newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia minister in Australia cash case quits.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia minister in Australia cash case quits.

text.p: Malaysian leader Muhammad Muhammad Taib, charged with attempting to take US$940,000 in foreign currency out of Australia, has quit as chief minister of Selangor state, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on Saturday.

Muhammad resigned at a meeting of the Supreme Council of Malaysia's dominant political party United Malay National Organisation (UMNO) on Saturday. His resignation will be effective from Monday, Mahathir said.

"It is his own wish to resign so that any investigation conducted will not affect UMNO's image and we will only consider his position in the party after the decision in Brisbane on whether he is guilty or not," Mahathir told reporters.

The Prime Minister said Muhammad made his decision after hearing the views of UMNO Supreme Council members during a discussion on corruption and abuse of power and position, the national Bernama news agency reported.

Asked whether Muhammad's decision reflected an admission of guilt, Mahathir said: "I don't know whether it is an admission of guilt. But what he stated is that he does not want UMNO to be linked in any of the investigation."
Muhammad, a vice-president of UMNO, is considered one of the country's most influential men. He has been chief minister of Selangor since August, 1986.
The Prime Minister said Muhammad's position as the UMNO vice-president would be decided only on Monday when the Selangor chief minister issues an official statement.
Bernama said Muhammad had also resigned as UMNO's liaison chief for Kuala Lumpur and Selangor and as chairman of Barisan Nasional, the ruling alliance, for the two regions.

Muhammad has said he was not aware of the Australian law requiring him to declare the money. He said the funds had been entrusted to him by his brothers for a property purchase on Brisbane's Gold Coast.
He has said the deal could not be concluded because his brothers could not be present and so the money was being taken back to Malaysia.
He was detained at the Brisbane International Airport on December 22 last year, after an equivalent of A$1.2 million ($940,000) in various currencies was found in his luggage.

At a preliminary hearing of the case in the Brisbane Magistrate's Court on Friday, Muhammad was charged with failing to declare to customs an amount over A$5,000 under the Financial Transactions Reports Act, 1988.
Muhammad, who was in Kuala Lumpur on Saturday, was not required to appear at Friday's hearing.
The transactions reports law carries a maximum fine of A$5,000 ($3,925) or a jail term not exceeding two years or both on conviction.
At the hearing, the prosecution said Muhammad will also face an additional charge of making a false declaration when his case comes up for hearing on August 19.
The additional charge, under the same Act, carries a maximum fine of A$10,000 ($7,850) or a jail term not exceeding five years or both on conviction. (A$1 = $0.785)
